title: Where victory lives
hookLine: the Gita ends with its narrator telling a blind king where victory really lies
carry: god's grace and your effort, together

lines: A BLIND KING IN HIS PALACE.
THE WHOLE GITA IS THE ANSWER.
cards: Go back to the very first verse. An old blind king, Dhritarashtra, sits in his palace far from the battlefield. His sons lead one army.
His nephews, Arjuna and his brothers, lead the other. He can't see, so he asks his charioteer Sanjaya, who has been given the gift of seeing far off: what are they doing?
The entire Gita, every word, has been Sanjaya's answer. The king was hoping for news of his sons. What he got was this.
Today, Sanjaya speaks for the last time.

teach.b: First, Arjuna. Verse seventy-three: my confusion is gone. I've found my memory again, through your grace.
I stand firm, my doubts are gone. I will do what you say. Karishye vachanam tava.
In chapter one he was shaking. Now he stands. Then Sanjaya.
Verse seventy-four: I have heard this wondrous conversation between Krishna and the great-souled Arjuna, and my hair stands on end.
Verse seventy-five: by the grace of Vyasa, the sage the Mahabharata names as its author, I heard this highest secret, this yoga, from Krishna, the lord of yoga himself, speaking it directly.
Verse seventy-six: remembering again and again this wondrous and holy dialogue, I rejoice, again and again. Verse seventy-seven: remembering that astonishing form of Hari, great is my wonder.
Then verse seventy-eight, the last verse of the Gita.
Wherever there is Krishna, the lord of yoga, wherever there is Arjuna, the archer, there is fortune, victory, well-being and sound judgment. That is my conviction.
It's quietly pointed: Sanjaya is telling a king who wanted his own sons to win exactly where victory lies. Krishna, the lord of yoga, holds the reins. Arjuna, bow in hand, does the fighting.
Many teachers read the verse as grace and effort together: not grace without effort, not effort without grace, but both in one chariot.
It's why many Hindus begin their work with a prayer, then put their whole effort in. The war still has to be fought; the Mahabharata goes on.

how: When Hindus recite the whole Gita, the reading closes with Sanjaya's words in 18.74–18.78; the last verse, on fortune and victory wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, is sometimes recited on its own as a blessing.

games.q: you're Sanjaya. the blind king wanted news of his sons' victory. what do you tell him at the very end?
o: wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, there is victory.
the outcome is unknown to me.
games.why: verse 78: wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, there is fortune and victory. that is my conviction.

practice: Do what Sanjaya does: remember. Let one moment from these weeks of the Gita come back to you: the lamp in a windless place, the upside-down tree, your own dharma. Then think of one thing you'll work at tomorrow.
If you pray, offer it before you start, as many Hindus do. If you don't, picture doing your full part, and leaving room for what you can't control.

orig.note: Sanskrit: vijaya, victory; one of the four gifts named in the Gita's last verse, 18.78.
